title: Projects: from a baseline to a working system
summary: Apply the curriculum through bounded projects with concrete artifacts and acceptance criteria.
html:
Apply the curriculum through bounded projects with concrete artifacts and acceptance criteria.

How the pieces connect

Project 1: structured-data baseline

Choose a public dataset with a documented target. Build a leakage-safe pipeline with a simple model, then compare a tree ensemble. Deliver a split manifest, data checks, model artifact, held-out metrics with uncertainty, and an error analysis. Success means reproducible evaluation, not the highest available score.

Project 2: evidence-grounded assistant

Index a small document collection with stable source IDs. Build lexical and dense retrieval baselines. Add generation only after measuring evidence recall. Deliver queries including unanswerable and adversarial cases, source-linked answers, access checks, and latency traces. Test missing evidence and stale documents explicitly.

Project 3: one kernel under a microscope

Implement or select a vector operation and a matrix multiplication. Predict FLOPs, bytes, and memory capacity. Measure warmed execution with appropriate synchronization. Change one factor—batch size, dtype, layout, or fusion—and explain the result using the GPU handbook. Report correctness and end-to-end time.

Project 4: evaluate a research claim

Choose a paper with accessible code and data. Reproduce one central table at a feasible scale, maintaining original settings where possible. Run an ablation and document deviations. Deliver environment details, artifacts, uncertainty, and a clear account of what reproduced and what did not.

Worked example

For a document assistant, a useful acceptance criterion is: on 50 versioned questions, required evidence is retrieved for at least the agreed target proportion; unsupported questions trigger abstention; every cited answer has a verified supporting passage. Set targets before evaluating and record the actual counts.

What goes wrong

A polished interface can hide a missing baseline, and a benchmark can hide a broken user flow. Test the entire intended task.

Check your understanding

What should a final project report include beyond its best score?

Reveal the explanation

Dataset and split identity, configuration, baseline, error cases, uncertainty, resource usage, limitations, and runnable artifacts.

An operating model for projects: from a baseline to a working system

A good capstone produces evidence, not just an interface. It should have an explicit baseline, a fixed evaluation set, run instructions, and a record of what failed. Choose a project small enough to finish the entire loop: collection, modeling, testing, deployment behavior, and a written assessment.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: the smallest credible AI project

A good capstone can be modest: a document assistant for one bounded corpus, a classifier for one decision, or a small control simulation. The test is whether the whole loop is present. Define the user decision and acceptance criterion, establish a simple baseline, version the data and configuration, measure the failure cases, and deliver a reproducible artifact with limitations. A polished interface without that evidence is a demo, not a project conclusion.

Write the report before the last experiment: problem boundary, data provenance, split, baseline, final configuration, metrics, latency or resource use, errors, and what would falsify the claim. This turns a project from a collection of code into an argument another person can inspect and extend.

Notebook: Write the claim before the result

Write the acceptance criteria before implementation. At the end, ask a peer to run the project from a clean environment and check whether the documented evidence supports the conclusion.

claim = "method improves retrieval recall"
metric = "top_10_evidence_recall"
baseline = evaluate(reference_system)
candidate = evaluate(new_system)
report(claim, baseline, candidate, seed, data_version)
What to test next. 1. Scope: Choose a bounded decision, data source, and acceptance criterion. 2. Baseline: Build a simple reproducible end-to-end version. 3. Evaluate: Measure quality, latency, cost, and failure cases. 4. Deliver: Package artifacts, evidence, limitations, and next steps.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Scope. Choose a bounded decision, data source, and acceptance criterion.
  2. Baseline. Build a simple reproducible end-to-end version.
  3. Evaluate. Measure quality, latency, cost, and failure cases.
  4. Deliver. Package artifacts, evidence, limitations, and next steps.

Write the acceptance criteria before implementation. At the end, ask a peer to run the project from a clean environment and check whether the documented evidence supports the conclusion.

Verification questions for projects: from a baseline to a working system

BoundaryQuestionEvidence
